## Paper

## Abstract

Precisely engineering metal-ion vacancy in dynamically reconstructed electrocatalysts provides an attractive symmetry-breaking tool to develop robust electrocatalysts under operation conditions. Herein, we demonstrate a convenient Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction strategy to fabricate Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH nanosheets under oxygen evolution reaction conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen for practical anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis. The Sr-ion substitution in pre-catalysts can weaken bond strength for facilitated Co-ion vacancies formation in reconstructed oxyhydroxides. These Co-ion vacancies not only strengthen Co-O covalency for lattice oxygen activation, but also improve hydroxyl affinity for lattice oxygen refilling. The corresponding water electrolyzer exhibits a cutting-edge current of 3.3 A cm-2 at 2.0 V with a lowered energy consumption of 43.5 kWh kg-1 H2, and negligible degradation of 0.10 mV h-1 for 1000 h. This work paves an enlightening guideline to finely engineer metal-ion vacancy in dynamically reconstructed electrocatalysts, demonstrating the feasibility to develop targeted catalysts under practical conditions.

---

## Introduction

The anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) is becoming highly attractive for industrial hydrogen production due to its facility of combining advantages of alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) and proton-exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), such as employing earth-abundant catalysts and affording high operating currents1–3. Nevertheless, the industry-scale application of AEMWE is largely limited by the lack of non-noble metal-based catalysts with both high activity and stability for sluggish oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at anode4,5. Although several non-noble 3d metal-based materials have been reported to be active relative to commercial Ir- and Ru-based oxides, most of them still suffer from dynamic reconstruction with severe degradation under long-term OER conditions6–8. Specially, cobalt oxyhydroxide (CoOOH), known as the real catalytic phase reconstructed from pristine Co-based materials under OER conditions9–11, has been recently identified as one of the most promising OER catalysts for practical utilization with a relatively slow degradation rate and adjustable activity12,13. To overcome the theoretically limited OER overpotential of 370 mV in traditional adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM)14–16, activation of lattice oxygen by improving metal-oxygen covalency has been revealed to trigger lattice-oxygen oxidation mechanism (LOM) for activity enhancement17–19. However, the generated oxygen deficiencies due to the participation of lattice oxygen always render the dissolution of adjacent lattice metal with structure collapse, leading to the degraded performance of catalysts under LOM route for long-term utilization20–22. Accordingly, it is challenging and fundamentally important to develop well-reconstructed Co-based catalysts under OER conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen for practical AEMWE.

As a typical symmetry-breaking structure, the construction of metal-ion vacancies has been recently recognized to make an adjustment in the local atomic configuration of metal-based catalysts with altered charge density gradient, thus resulting in distinct catalytic behaviors23–25. For instance, Wang and co-workers demonstrated that the La-ion vacancy in LaFeO3 can greatly enhance the mobility of lattice oxygen due to the decreased electron density, subsequently reducing the barrier for C-H cleavage and oxidation of methane to generate syngas26. Of note, almost all the current efforts have been made to develop strategies to fabricate metal-ion vacancies in as-synthesized nanomaterials, while the inevitably dynamic reconstruction of metal-based catalysts under operation conditions could rebuild the local atomic structures with vanished vacancy sites27–29. For example, Magnussen et al. observed the dynamic reconstruction of Cu catalysts from low-coordinated Cu nanoclusters into isolated Cu atoms with increased potentials during electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR)30. Yang et al. proved the electrochemical reconstruction of Cu single atoms in C3N4 to Cu nanoparticles as the active phase for C2+ products during CO2RR31. As such, the precise design of metal-ion vacancies in dynamically reconstructed metal-based catalysts deserves to be investigated, which could serve as a versatile tool to develop high-performance catalysts under practical conditions.

Here, we demonstrate a facile Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction strategy to synthesize Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH nanosheets under OER conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen as efficient and stable anodic catalysts for practical AEMWE. Mechanistic investigations unveiled that Sr-ion substitution in selenide pre-catalysts could largely weaken the bond strength for accelerated reconstruction under OER conditions, contributing to the generation of abundant Co-ion vacancy in reconstructed oxyhydroxides. These Co-ion vacancies not only strengthened valence-electron sharing between Co and O sites with enhanced covalency for lattice oxygen activation with triggered LOM route, but also promoted valence-electron interaction between Co sites and OH adsorbates with enhanced hydroxyl affinity for lattice oxygen refilling during LOM route. Accordingly, these catalysts served as promising anodic OER catalysts for AEMWE. Relative to CoOOH and commercial RuO2, the Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH nanosheets showed an 18.6-fold and 25.0-fold increase in OER currents, respectively, as well as a significantly promoted OER stability with only 2% degradation in overpotentials after 10000 accelerated potential cycles. Practical testing in AEMWE presented a cutting-edge cell voltage of 2.0 V to achieve 3.3 A cm−2 with a lowered energy consumption of 43.5 kWh kg−1 H2, and a good operation stability with a negligible degradation rate of 0.10 mV h−1 for 1000 h, outperforming commercial RuO2. The competitive AEMWE performance further identified the compatibility of Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH for practical utilization.

---

## Results

To begin with, Sr-ion-substituted CoSe2 nanobelts with weakened bond strength (denoted as Sr-CoSe2-w) were synthesized and serve as the pre-catalysts before electrochemical reconstruction (Fig. 1a). As theoretically calculated in the well-established Sr-ion-substituted CoSe2 and pure CoSe2 models (Supplementary Fig. 1), the Co-Se bond length around Sr sites exhibited an obvious increase (Supplementary Fig. 2a), together with the decreased Se vacancy formation energy with Sr substitution (Supplementary Fig. 2b), suggesting the weakened Co-Se bonding by Sr substitution. These selenides possessed smooth and belt-like morphology with uniform distribution of Co, Se, and Sr, as identified by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Fig. 1b), and high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) with elemental mapping (Fig. 1c). The Sr/Co molar ratio was determined as 1.0% by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). The aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM image clearly suggested the well-maintained cubic CoSe2 structure of 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w32, where the Sr-ion substitution can be confirmed by the intensity profiles of selected region (Fig. 1d). Similarly, by varying added amounts of precursors, 0.6%Sr-CoSe2-w, 0.2%Sr-CoSe2-w and pure CoSe2 pre-catalysts with uniform morphology and cubic phase were obtained (Supplementary Fig. 3). The Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra and fitting results demonstrated the largely reduced Co-Se coordination from 3.9 for pure CoSe2 to 2.3 for 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w, as well as the obviously increased Co-Se bond length after Sr substitution (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 1). These results clearly suggested the largely weakened bond strength in these selenides through Sr-ion substitution. To deeply understand the weakened Co-Se bond caused by Sr-ion substitution, the valence-electron states were analyzed. The Co 2p X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum for 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w exhibited two typical peaks at 778.5 eV and 793.4 eV that assigned to Co-Se bond in cubic CoSe233. Obviously, a negative shift of Co 2p peaks to low energy was observed on going from pure CoSe2 to 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w (Fig. 1f), indicating the enriched valence-electron density of Co sites with Sr-ion substitution. Meanwhile, a positive shift of Sr 3d XPS peaks of Sr-Se bond was also found with increased Sr/Co ratio from 0.2% to 1.0% (Supplementary Fig. 4)34. These results suggested the substituted Sr atoms in selenide pre-catalysts could supply electrons more efficiently than Co atoms to bond Se sites, in accordance with the difference of work functions, thus accounting for the weakened Co-Se bond strength.

The weakened bond strength in Sr-CoSe2-w pre-catalysts endowed a lowered dissociation energy of Co-Se bond relative to that in pure CoSe235,36, which could accelerate the bond dissociation under the attack of OH- ions from alkaline electrolyte with forming low-coordinated Co sites during reconstruction, reasonably facilitating the formation of abundant Co-ion vacancies in the reconstructed oxyhydroxide catalysts (Fig. 2a). To clarify the reconstruction process, in situ Raman analysis was conducted under a series of potential cycles (Supplementary Fig. 5). As shown in Fig. 2b, the Raman spectra of pristine 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w pre-catalysts showcased three typical peaks at 476, 517 and 683 cm−1 assigned to cubic CoSe2 phase37. As the potential cycles proceeded, these peaks tended to vanish, together with the formation of another two peaks at 498 and 594 cm−1 assigned to Eg and A1g vibrational modes of Co-O in CoOOH (Supplementary Fig. 6)38, as well as the gradually elevated Co oxidation state to ~3 (Fig. 2c), manifesting the complete reconstruction from selenide to oxyhydroxide phase. Relative to the pre-catalysts without Sr-ion substitution, the Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction can be notably accelerated, as proved by the obviously reduced potential cycles for reconstruction. The morphology of reconstructed oxyhydroxides was characterized by TEM (Fig. 2d), where interconnected nanosheets with massive boundaries were observed. Such boundaries could facilitate the generation of low-coordination vacancies in these Sr-ion-substituted oxyhydroxide nanosheets39. For simplicity, we designated them as Sr-CoOOH nanosheets. The STEM image and element mapping exhibited homogeneous distribution of Co and Sr in these nanosheets (Fig. 2e), where the Sr/Co ratio was maintained as 1.0% by ICP-OES. The atomic structure was further visualized by an aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM image (Fig. 2f). The bright spots marked by yellow circles clearly suggested the substituted Sr atoms, while the diffraction rings in the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern suggested the amorphous structure. The atomic dispersion of these Sr atoms could also be verified by the absence of Sr-Sr coordination in Sr K-edge EXAFS spectra (Fig. 2g). Similar morphology and amorphous structures were also observed in other reconstructed Sr-CoOOH nanosheets with maintained Sr/Co ratios of 0.2% and 0.6%, as evidenced by the TEM images, HRTEM images, XRD patterns and ICP-OES analysis (Supplementary Figs. 7, 8).

To verify the local coordination environment in these Sr-CoOOH nanosheets, Co K-edge EXAFS measurements were conducted (Fig. 2h). All the Sr-CoOOH nanosheets exhibited two main peaks at around 1.5 Å and 2.5 Å, attributing to Co-O and Co-Co bonds for CoOOH, respectively40. Notably, with increased Sr contents, a shrinkage of Co-O bond length was observed, suggesting the enhanced Co-O covalency. The strengthened Co-O covalency could efficiently activate lattice oxygen to trigger the LOM pathway for bypassing the theoretically limited OER overpotential41. Meanwhile, least-squares fittings were performed to quantitatively understand the coordination structure (Supplementary Table 2). As collected in Fig. 2i, the Co-Co coordination numbers decreased from 3.0 for CoOOH to 2.7 for 0.2%Sr-CoOOH, 2.6 for 0.6%Sr-CoOOH, and 2.4 for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, together with the well-maintained Co-O coordination numbers, clearly demonstrating the formation of abundant Co vacancies by Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction. In addition, such the construction of metal-ion vacancies by Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction could also be extended to other reconstructed metal-based materials (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10 and Table 3), suggesting the Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction method as a useful tool to realize metal-ion vacancies in dynamically reconstructed catalysts.

The valence electron properties of the Sr-CoOOH nanosheets were characterized by XPS analysis. As shown in Fig. 2j, the Co 2p3/2 XPS peaks at 779.9 eV and 781.1 eV corresponded to the Co3+ cations in CoOOH42, while a positive shift of Co 2p peaks to high energy was observed from pure CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH. Meanwhile, the Sr 3d XPS spectra, which were divided into two peaks at 133.4 and 135.1 eV for Sr cations43 and in accordance with the cationic nature from Sr K-edge XANES spectra (Supplementary Fig. 11a), showed a negative shift to low energy from 0.2%Sr-CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH (Supplementary Fig. 11b). The decreased valence-electron density of Co sites and increased valence-electron density of Sr sites implied enhanced valence-electron interaction of Co-O bonds in Sr-CoOOH (Supplementary Table 4), in accordance with the elevated Co-O covalency. The electron state of O sites was studied by O 1s XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 12), which could be fitted into four contributions from O-Co bonds (529.7 eV), OH-Co bonds (530.8 eV), low-coordination O (OL, 531.5 eV) and adsorbed water (H2Oad, 532.1 eV)44. The corresponding contents were collected in Fig. 2k. Of note, an obvious increase of O-Co bonds can be observed from pure CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, which could be attributed to the enhanced Co-O covalency and elevated structure stabilization due to the higher bond dissociation energy of Sr-O bond (454 kJ mol−1) than Co-O bond (368 kJ mol−1)45. The decreased OH-Co bonds and retained low-coordination O consisted with the increased Co vacancies and retained Co-O coordination from CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH. Moreover, the increased O contents for water adsorption indicated the elevated affinity of oxygenous species of Sr-CoOOH, which could accelerate the refilling process of lattice oxygen during OER.

The electrocatalytic OER performance of all the Sr-CoOOH catalysts were investigated in O2-saturated 1 M KOH electrolyte. As illustrated by the polarization curves in Fig. 3a, which were all corrected for the ohmic loss (Supplementary Fig. 13), 1.0%Sr-CoOOH exhibited the earliest onset potential and an overpotential as low as 255 mV at 10 mA cm−2, significantly outperforming that of 312 mV for pure CoOOH and 327 mV for commercial RuO2. Notably, 1.0%Sr-CoOOH can achieve the current density of 100 mA cm−2 with a low overpotential of 293 mV (Fig. 3b), which was 5.0, 8.8, 18.6, and 25.0 times higher than that for 0.6%Sr-CoOOH, 0.2%Sr-CoOOH, pure CoOOH, and commercial RuO2, respectively. Meanwhile, the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, achieved by the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) measurements (Supplementary Figs. 14, 15), showed only the 1.1, 1.8, and 2.7-fold increase relative to that for 0.6%Sr-CoOOH, 0.2%Sr-CoOOH, and pure CoOOH, respectively. Obviously, the current increase for these samples was much larger than the variation of ECSA, suggesting the remarkably enhanced intrinsic activity. The activity elevation was further verified by the Tafel plot and turnover frequency (TOF) analysis. Figure 3c displays a much lowered Tafel slope of 38 mV dec−1 for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH relative to 0.6%Sr-CoOOH (46 mV dec−1), 0.2%Sr-CoOOH (65 mV dec−1), CoOOH (70 mV dec−1) and commercial RuO2 (117 mV dec−1), indicating the accelerated reaction kinetics. The TOF values for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH also remained higher than those for all the tested samples throughout applied potentials, further implying the intrinsically boosted OER activity (Fig. 3d). Of note, the OER activity of 1.0%Sr-CoOOH was competitive (Supplementary Table 5), and could further afford a more competitive target on the gas diffusion electrode with a significantly lowered overpotential of 198 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and a Tafel slope of 32 mV dec−1 as the efficient Co-based OER catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 16).

The stability of these Sr-CoOOH catalysts under OER conditions were systematically elucidated. To understand the operating stability, we conducted galvanostatic start-stop measurements at 10 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3e). For 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, the voltages at 10 mA cm−2 showed neglectable variation during repeated start-stop tests, implying the attractive stability for practical operation46. The long-term stability was assessed by means of accelerated voltammetry cycling tests (Fig. 3f). In comparison with the significantly degraded activities of pure CoOOH under long-term cycling, the activity of 1.0%Sr-CoOOH showed negligible variation after 10000 potential cycles. As quantitatively summarized in Fig. 3g, the overpotentials for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH to achieve 10 mA cm−2 only exhibited a 2% increase after 10000 scan cycles, much lower than the 35% increase in overpotentials for pure CoOOH and thus indicating the high stability of Sr-CoOOH for long-term utilization. The dissolution of metal ions under different scan cycles was also measured by ICP-OES to further evaluate the stability (Fig. 3h). For pure CoOOH, Co components dissolved obviously after 2000 cycles and showed a 49% decrease in content after 10000 cycles. For 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, these Co components were basically retained during the long-term cycling with only 4% decrease in content after 10000 cycles, clearly suggesting the improved stability of Sr-CoOOH. The structural stability was further demonstrated by the well-maintained Sr/Co molar ratios in 1.0%Sr-CoOOH during long-term cycling, as well as the well-maintained morphology from TEM image (Supplementary Fig. 17a), amorphous phase from HRTEM image (Supplementary Fig. 17b) and XRD patterns (Supplementary Fig. 17c), and stable valence states of Co, Sr, O sites from XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 17d–f). The high stability of 1.0%Sr-CoOOH also ensured sufficient exposure of active sites for long-term OER catalysis, as verified by the well-maintained ECSAs during long-term cycling (Supplementary Figs. 18, 19 and Fig. 3i).

Considering the enhanced Co-O covalency can trigger the switch of OER route from AEM to LOM for activity improvement, the reaction mechanism for these Sr-CoOOH catalysts were experimentally evaluated. Figure 4a shows the in situ Raman spectra for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH during the real-time OER process with applied potentials. At the open-circuit potential (OCP), two typical peaks at 498 and 594 cm−1 were visible, in accordance with Co-O stretching of amorphous CoOOH. When the applied potential increased, these two peaks shifted to 477 and 574 cm−1 as the Co-O stretching of CoO247, together with the generation of a new peak at 1064 cm−1 for superoxide O-O bands with the participation of lattice oxygen48, suggesting the occurrence of the LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH containing the deprotonation and immediate coupling with lattice oxygen. For comparison, potential-dependent Raman spectra for pure CoOOH were also detected (Fig. 4b). The absence of peaks at around 1064 cm−1 indicated the different OER pathway for pure CoOOH from the LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH. Besides, the variation of Co sites could also be verified by XANES spectra (Supplementary Fig. 20), where the increased oxidation states of Co with applied potentials were clearly observed. Of note, with applied potential back to OCP, both of these samples exhibited a reversed Co oxidation state to ~3, together with the well-maintained coordination structure around Co sites (Supplementary Fig. 21 and Table 6, 7), suggesting the stable Co active sites in these oxyhydroxide catalysts for the OER process. To further identify the OER route, the pH-dependent activities were tested. With pH values decreased from 14.0 to 12.5, the OER activities for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH exhibited a significant decrease (Fig. 4c), while pure CoOOH only showed a tiny variation (Fig. 4d). To precisely clarify the correlation between pH and activity, the proton reaction order on RHE scale (ρRHE) was calculated (Fig. 4e), where the concerted proton-electron-transfer process tends to be zeroth-order49. Notably, the ρRHE value of 0.84 for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH was much larger than that of 0.04 for pure CoOOH, suggesting the triggered LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH from the AEM route for CoOOH50–52. Furthermore, to track the O-O coupling species generated with a negative charge in a non-concerted proton-electron-transfer LOM route, tetramethylammonium cation (TMA+) was introduced into the electrolyte as a probe due to its specific interaction with negative oxygenated species for hindered OER kinetics53. As shown in Fig. 4f, the 1.0%Sr-CoOOH showed obviously reduced OER activity in 1 M TMAOH relative to 1 M KOH, together with the increased Tafel slope from 38 to 65 mV dec−1, confirming the LOM route occurred with strong binding of TMA+ on O2- species. For pure CoOOH, only a slight change in activities was observed (Fig. 4g), indicating the AEM route. The binding behaviors of TMA+ were also detected by Raman spectra (Fig. 4h). Besides the two peaks at 498 and 594 cm–1 referring to CoOOH phase for both samples, two new peaks at 752 and 954 cm−1 corresponding to TMA+ were only observed on 1.0%Sr-CoOOH under 1.50 V in TMAOH54, further indicating the switched LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH from AEM route for pure CoOOH (Fig. 4i).

To gain an in-depth understanding on the intrinsic reason for switching pathway with activity enhancement as well as the improvement of stability, we conducted first-principles calculations using DFT. The models of Sr-CoOOH and pure CoOOH were well-established in Supplementary Data 1, Figs. 22, 23, and Table 8, where another Sr-CoOOH flat surface without Co vacancy was also constructed for comparison, and denoted as Sr-CoOOHf. Figure 5a shows the change of valence-electron density of Co sites in these structures. The inhomogeneity of electron loss at each Co sites in pure CoOOH could be attributed to the Jahn-Teller distortion. Relative to pure CoOOH, the Sr substitution in Sr-CoOOHf induced increased electron loss from adjacent Co sites, which could be attributed to the limited valence-electron providing ability of Sr to bond O and thus the increased valence-electron supply from adjacent Co sites. As such, further introduction of Co vacancy would induce extra valence-electron supply from adjacent Co sites to bond O, which was also suggested by the extra electron loss of Co sites in Sr-CoOOHv. The increased valence-electron sharing between Co and O could reasonably shorten the adjacent Co-O bonds (Supplementary Fig. 24) with enhanced covalency, in accordance with the XPS and EXAFS results. The enhanced Co-O covalency was further verified by the projected density of states (pDOS) with averaging the potential Co and O sites (Supplementary Fig. 25). As presented in Fig. 5b, relative to pure CoOOH, the Sr substitution in Sr-CoOOHf could diminish the difference between Co 3d band center (εd) and O 2p band center (εp) from 0.335 eV to 0.167 eV, indicating the partially promoted covalency. Meanwhile, with further introduction of Co vacancy in Sr-CoOOHv, the d band of Co and p band of O exhibited a further shortened band-center difference of 0.127 eV, indicating that the Co vacancy could enhance the Co-O covalency and thus lead to the efficient lattice oxygen activation for triggering the LOM pathway. The reaction sites for LOM could be further verified by calculating the energy difference of the potential-determining step (PDS, Supplementary Fig. 26). In view of the obvious difference of step I between AEM and LOM pathways (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 27), the activation barriers from the AEM intermediate of adsorbed O after step I to the LOM intermediate after step I for O-O coupling were then assessed to clarify the switch difficulty of OER pathways. As shown in Fig. 5d, the energy barrier from AEM intermediate to the isomeric LOM intermediate after step I was 0.51 eV for Sr-CoOOHv, obviously lower than that of 1.52 eV for Sr-CoOOHf and 1.68 eV for pure CoOOH (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 28), and thus indicating the facilitated switch of OER route from AEM to LOM for Sr-CoOOHv with rich Co vacancies. The switched route from AEM to LOM because of the lattice oxygen activation could boost the theoretically plagued OER kinetics by overcoming the linear relation of OH* and OOH* with direct O-O coupling55. To clarify the role of the altered OER pathway in activity, the relevant Gibbs free energies for reaction steps on Sr-CoOOHv and CoOOH were further depicted. For both structures in Fig. 5f, g, the deprotonation of OH* (step I) in the AEM route or the deprotonation of OH* with immediate O-O coupling (step I) in the LOM route could serve as the potential-determining step. For CoOOH, the energy barrier of 2.01 eV of PDS in the AEM route was lower than that of 2.63 eV in the LOM route, suggesting the OER process follows the AEM route. A similar AEM route could also be observed for Sr-CoOOHf (Supplementary Fig. 29), identifying the deficient activation of lattice oxygen only by Sr substitution. In contrast, for Sr-CoOOHv, the PDS energy in the AEM route was higher than that in the LOM pathway, even under varied U values (Supplementary Fig. 30), reflecting the switched LOM route for Sr-CoOOHv. Moreover, the well-established Sr-CoOOHv exhibited an obviously lowered PDS energy barrier of 1.58 eV than that of 2.01 eV for pure CoOOH, as well as those for the other configurations with varied position of Co vacancy sites (Supplementary Figs. 31, 32), indicating the intrinsically accelerated OER process for Sr-CoOOHv with switched LOM route.

Considering the release of lattice oxygen involving in the LOM route would dynamically generate oxygen deficiencies in catalysts and result in structural collapse, it is of significant importance to efficiently refill these lattice oxygen deficiencies during the LOM route for long-term stability56. Accordingly, the behaviors for lattice oxygen refilling in the LOM route on Sr-CoOOHv and CoOOH were analyzed. Relative to pure CoOOH, the Co-Co coordination missing in Sr-CoOOHv with abundant Co vacancies and Sr substitution with limited valence-electron providing ability could narrow the d band of adjacent Co sites due to the reduced Co d-band overlap, as verified by the upshifted d-band center (Fig. 5b) and the calculated d-band width57, and thus leading to the strengthened OH adsorption affinity for Sr-CoOOHv. To clearly understand the behaviors for lattice oxygen refilling in the LOM route, the electron density differences of intermediate structures of Sr-CoOOHv and CoOOH for lattice oxygen refilling with OH adsorbates were analyzed. As illustrated in Fig. 5h, relative to pure CoOOH, the Co vacancy in Sr-CoOOHv could trigger an enhanced valence-electron interaction between adjacent Co sites and OH adsorbates to refill the lattice oxygen deficiency generated during the LOM route, indicating the promoted lattice oxygen refilling ability of Sr-CoOOHv with Co vacancies. The efficient lattice oxygen refilling was further verified by the energy barrier calculation (Fig. 5i). Notably, the Sr-CoOOHv still exhibited a lower energy barrier of 0.79 eV for incorporating O into the lattice than that of 1.20 eV for pure CoOOH, suggesting the efficient refilling ability of lattice oxygen of Sr-CoOOHv and thus the strengthened OER stability. The structure stability under OER conditions could be further proved by the electrochemical phase diagram58–60, where Sr-CoOOHv could exhibit obviously enhanced stability with much-lowered formation free energy with respect to pure CoOOH (Supplementary Fig. 33).

The boosted activity with efficient lattice oxygen activation and strengthened stability with efficient lattice oxygen refilling of Sr-CoOOHv suggest its attractive potential for realistic utilization as anodic OER catalysts. To this end, we conducted the tests in an anion-exchange membrane electrolyzer at 80 °C with 1 M KOH as feed and commercial Pt/C as cathodic catalysts (Supplementary Figs. 34, 35). Polarization curves were collected in Fig. 6a. Notably, the AEMWE with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode achieved a remarkably high current density of 3.3 A cm−2 with a much-lowered voltage of 2.0 V, clearly outperforming the pure CoOOH anode with a current density of 1.9 A cm−2 at 2.0 V, as well as the commercial RuO2 anode with a current density of 0.63 A cm−2 at 2.0 V. Moreover, at 1.0 A cm−2, the AEMWE with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode produced 1.78 L of H2 at the running electrolyzer for 1 h. The energy consumption of the AEMWE device was deduced to be 43.5 kWh kg−1 H2 (Fig. 6b), obviously lower than that of CoOOH and the goal of 47.9 kWh kg−1 H2 from the Office of Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy (EERE) in the US Department of Energy (DOE). The Faradaic efficiency of O2 product in the AEMWE device with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode was quantified as a near unity value of 99.3% (Fig. 6c), suggesting the entire consumption of charge without parasitic reactions. To further confirm the applicability of the electrolyzer assembled with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv, the operating stability measurements were performed in AEMWE at a constant industrial-level current density of 500 mA cm−2 under 80 °C. As shown in Fig. 6d, the AEMWE with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode presented a well-maintained performance during 1000 h electrolysis with a negligible degradation rate of 0.10 mV h−1, significantly lower than that of 1.33 mV h−1 during 95 h electrolysis on a commercial RuO2 anode and implying the improved stability. The overall performance of the AEMWE device with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode, including current density at 2.0 V, operating time and degradation rate, were competitive with using a commercial anion-exchange membrane and a commercial Pt/C cathode (Supplementary Table 9).

## Methods

Chemicals
Cobalt(II) acetate tetrahydrate (Co(AC)2·4H2O, ≥99.5%), strontium acetate (Sr(AC)2, 99%), sodium selenite (Na2SeO3, ≥97.0%), isopropanol (C3H8O, ≥99.7%), ethanol (C2H6OH, ≥99.7%), diethylenetriamine (DETA, ≥98.5%), and potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥85.0%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd (Shanghai, China). Ruthenium dioxide (RuO2, 99.9%) and Tetramethylammonium hydroxide solution (TMAOH, 25 wt% in H2O) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ) was used in all the experiments.

Materials preparation
The Sr-CoOOHv nanosheets rich in Co vacancies were prepared in two steps. To begin with, the Sr-CoSe2-w nanobelts were synthesized as pre-catalysts by a facile hydrothermal method. In brief, 247.1 mg of Co(AC)2·4H2O, 1.62 mg of Sr(AC)2, and 173 mg of Na2SeO3 were dispersed in 40 mL of mixed solution containing DETA and DI water with a volume ratio of 2:1. The mixture was heated to 180 °C for 16 h to obtain the 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w samples. Sr/Co atomic ratios were controlled by varying the amount of two precursors without changing other conditions. Specifically, we added 249 mg of Co(AC)2·4H2O for pure CoSe2, 248.7 mg of Co(AC)2·4H2O and 0.32 mg of Sr(AC)2 for 0.2%Sr-CoSe2-w, as well as 247.8 mg of Co(AC)2·4H2O and 0.97 mg of Sr(AC)2 for 0.6%Sr-CoSe2-w, respectively. Then, for the preparation of Sr-CoOOHv nanosheets, we performed the electrochemical reconstruction of selenide pre-catalysts in O2-saturated 1 M KOH solution via a typical cyclic voltammetry cycling method between 1.02 and 1.5 V (vs. RHE) with a sweep rate of 50 mV s−1 and forty potential cycles. After being washed with DI water and ethanol, Sr-CoOOHv nanosheets were obtained.

XAS characterization
The X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was collected from the TLS 13B2 beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center (NSRRC) in Hsinchu, Taiwan. The storage of TLS worked at 1.5 GeV with a beam current of 360 mA. The X-ray pre- and post-edge absorptions were normalized to 0 and 1, respectively.

DFT calculations
The first-principles calculations were carried out using the spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) within the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation (GGA), implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The projected augmented wave (PAW) method was employed with a plane-wave cutoff energy of 520 eV. To prevent interactions between periodic images, a vacuum layer of approximately 15 Å was introduced along the z-axis in all slab models. The lattice constants and atomic positions were fully relaxed until the forces on each atom were below 0.02 eV/Å, with the total energy convergence criterion of 1×10−5 eV.

For selenide raw structures, the models were constructed by periodically repeating the CoSe2 (210) slab with three layers containing 72 atoms. The Brillouin zone was sampled using a 3×3×1 k-point grid. For pure CoOOH, the CoOOH(001) surface was simulated, which comprises two cobalt oxide layers slab with each layer containing 32 Co, 64 O and 32 H atoms. To account for van der Waals interactions between CoOOH layers, Grimme’s DFT-D3 semi-empirical method was adopted. In the geometric optimization, all atoms except those in the bottom layer were fully relaxed. For improved accuracy in describing Co 3d electrons, a Hubbard U term (Ueff = 3.3 eV) was corrected. For Sr-substituted CoOOH, we simulated the substitution of one Co atom with a Sr atom on the surface. For Sr-substituted CoOOH rich in Co vacancies, different Co vacancy configurations were considered, including nearest neighbor, next-nearest neighbor, and third-nearest neighbor positions relative to the Sr site. Due to the large unit cell and computational limitations, the Brillouin zone was sampled only at the Γ point.

The Gibbs free energy changes for water oxidation steps following the AEM mechanism were calculated as ref. 56
ΔG1 = ΔG(O*) − ΔG(OH*) (1)
ΔG2 = ΔG(OOH*) − ΔG(O*) (2)
ΔG3 = ΔG(OO*) − ΔG(OOH*) (3)
ΔG4 = 4.92 eV − ΔG(OO*) (4)
ΔG5 = ΔG(OH*) (5)

The Gibbs free energy changes for water oxidation steps following the LOM mechanism were calculated as:
ΔG1 = ΔG(OO*) − ΔG(OH*) (6)
ΔG2 = ΔG([OO+HO]*) − ΔG(OO*) (7)
ΔG3 = 4.92 eV + ΔG([Ov+HO]*) − ΔG([OO+HO]*) (8)
ΔG4 = ΔG(OHv*) − ΔG([Ov+HO]*) (9)
ΔG5 = ΔG(OH*) − ΔG(OHv*) (10)

The Gibbs free energy differences of these intermediates include zero-point energy (ZPE) and entropy corrections were calculated as:
ΔG = ΔE + ΔZPE − TΔS (11)

where the energy differences ΔE were calculated with respect to H2O and H2, and the vibrational entropy changes ΔS were calculated at 298.15 K. The detailed correction values were listed in Supplementary Table 10–12. The climbing image nudged elastic band method was used to search the transition state (TS).

Electrochemical measurements
The electrochemical measurements were taken on a standard three-electrode system in 175 mL of 1 M KOH (pH = 14.0 ± 0.01) using a CHI 760E electrochemical workstation by using a graphite rod and Hg/HgO electrode as the counter and reference electrode at room temperature (25 ± 1 °C), respectively. The 1 M KOH electrolyte was prepared freshly with dissolving 56.11 g of KOH in 1 L of DI water. The potentials in this work were referenced to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), and in 1 M KOH, ERHE = EHg/HgO + 0.903 V. The reference electrode calibration was conducted by using a typical cyclic voltammetry (CV) method within a three-electrode system in 1 M KOH saturated with high-purity hydrogen, where two Pt meshes served as the working and counter electrode, respectively. The CV curve was recorded at the sweep rate of 1 mV s−1, and the average value of the two potentials where the current crossed zero was taken as the calibration value.

For the preparation of the working electrode, 5 mg of catalyst powders and 1 mg of Ketjen black (KB) were dispersed in 1 mL mixed solution consisted of isopropanol and 5 wt% Nafion solution. Then 39.2 μL of the ink was dropped onto the glass carbon rotating disk electrode (RDE, 5 mm in diameter) with a mass loading of catalyst of 1 mg cm−2.

Before OER tests, the electrolyte was degassed for at least 30 min by oxygen bubbling. The polarization curves were collected with a sweep rate of 5 mV s−1 at a rotating speed of 1600 rpm, which were all corrected for the ohmic loss. The R values measured for 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv, 0.6%Sr-CoOOHv, 0.2%Sr-CoOOHv, and CoOOH were 7.2 ± 0.5, 6.8 ± 0.2, 6.0 ± 0.3, and 7.0 ± 0.2 Ω, respectively. The accelerated stability tests were performed by potential cycling between 1.2 and 1.48 V (vs. RHE) at a sweep rate of 100 mV s−1. The electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) was measured by using cyclic voltammetry within the potential region of 1.205-1.305 V (vs. RHE) at varied scan rates from 35 to 55 mV s−1. The linear slope was obtained by plotting the charging current density differences (Δj = ja − jc) against scan rates, which is twice of the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) and used to represent ECSA.

The turnover frequency (TOF) was calculated from the equation below:
TOF = 4 × j × F / A × n (12)
where j is the measured current density, A is the surface area of the electrode, F is the Faraday constant, and n is the moles of metal atoms on the electrode calculated from XPS results.

AEMWE measurements
The anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer (AEMWE) was assembled with the anode (Sr-CoOOHv, CoOOH, or RuO2), cathode (commercial Pt/C), and anion exchange membrane (PiperION, 40 μm in thickness). To prepare the anodic catalyst ink, the catalysts were homogeneously dispersed in a mixed solution containing DI water, isopropanol and ionomer under ultrasonication. Then the well-dispersed ink was sprayed on nickel foam with a loading mass of 5 mg cm−2. The cathodic catalyst (Pt/C, 40 wt% loading, Johnson Matthey) ink was prepared in the same method and sprayed on the carbon paper with a loading mass of Pt/C catalysts of 1 mg cm−2. Subsequently, these cathode and anode were sandwiched with the anion exchange membrane in a fixture with the applied torque of 3 N·m. The performance of the AEM electrolyzer was recorded in a continuously circulated 1 M KOH solution at an operation temperature of 80 °C. The stability test was recorded using galvanostatic electrolysis at a constant current density of 500 mA cm−2.

The energy consumption of the AEMWE is calculated by the following:
Energy consumption = Ucell × Icell × t / m (13)
where Icell is the current delivered (A), t is the operation time (h), and m is the mass of hydrogen produced in the operation process. Three independent measurements were conducted to achieve the standard deviation of the energy consumption.

The Faradaic efficiency was calculated from the amount of charge passed through the electrolyzer and the amount of oxygen produced as follows:
Faradaic efficiency = n × F × m / Q (14)
where F is the Faraday constant, n is 4 for the electron transfer in OER process, m is the moles of O2 gas produced at 1 A cm−2, and Q is the amount of charge passed. Three independent measurements were conducted to obtain the standard deviation of the Faradaic efficiency.

In situ Raman measurements
For detecting the dynamic reconstruction process, the in situ Raman spectra were conducted by Raman microscope (RENISHAW inVia Qontor) with 50xL (NA = 0.5) objective and 532 nm laser with 1800 l/mm optical grating. The samples were used as working electrodes, together with Pt wire and Hg/HgO as counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. The in situ Raman spectra of different potential cycles were recorded 3 times for 10 s to study the reconstructed process. For detecting the reaction route, the in situ Raman spectra of different applied voltages from 1.20 V to 1.50 V were recorded 10 times for 30 s to study the OER process, which was conducted by using the 785 nm laser and 1200 l/mm optical grating.

Characterization techniques
The Talos L120C G2 transmission electron microscope with an acceleration voltage of 120 kV was used to characterize the morphology of samples. The field-emission transmission electron microscope (Talos F200x) with 200 kV acceleration voltage was used to collect HRTEM images, HAADF-STEM images, and elemental mapping images. The AC HAADF-STEM images were achieved by using the spherical aberration corrected JEM-ARM300F2 microscope with 300 kV accelerating voltage. The X-ray diffractometer (XRD-6100, SHIMADZU) with a Cu-Kα radiation source was used to collect XRD patterns of samples. XAS spectra under varied conditions were collected on the XAS spectrometer (Table XAFS-500A, Specreation Instruments Co. Ltd.). XPS spectra were collected by using the X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (K-alpha, Thermo Scientific) with a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source. ICP-OES (Agilent 5110) was used to detect the content of Co and Sr elements.

oxygenated species with hindered OER kinetics (Nat. Energy 4, 329-338, (2019)). As such, the
TMA+ can be used to track the O-O coupling species in negative charge generated in LOM route
and thus identify the LOM route.

in the field of developing high-performance catalysts under practical conditions. As a typical
symmetry-breaking structure, constructing metal-ion vacancies has been recently recognized to
make an adjustment in local atomic configuration of metal-based catalysts with altered charge
density gradient for distinct catalytic behaviors. However, almost all the current efforts have been

the inevitably dynamic reconstruction for metal-based catalysts under operation conditions,
especially for the non-noble 3d metal-based materials under the highly corrosive alkaline OER

the uncontrollable catalytic performance. Moreover, the generated oxygen deficiencies due to the

“7. The OER performance is very poor, and the method for catalyst preparation is not new. Can
they provide some new points on their manuscript?”
We genuinely thank the reviewer for this suggestion. The new points that have been demonstrated
in our work are as follows:
i) We demonstrate a new Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction method to finely engineer Co-ion vacancy
in dynamically reconstructed CoOOH electrocatalyst under OER conditions. As a typical
symmetry-breaking structure, the construction of metal-ion vacancies has been recently recognized
to make an adjustment in local atomic configuration of metal-based catalysts with altered charge
density gradient, thus resulting in distinct catalytic behaviors. However, almost all the current
efforts have been made to develop strategies to fabricate metal-ion vacancies in as-synthesized
nanomaterials, while the inevitably dynamic reconstruction for metal-based catalysts under
operation conditions, especially for the non-noble 3d metal-based materials under the highly
corrosive alkaline OER conditions, could rebuild the local atomic structures with vanished vacancy
sites, leading to the uncontrollable catalytic performance. Accordingly, precise design of metal-
ion vacancies in dynamically reconstructed metal-based catalysts deserves to be investigated,
which could serve as a versatile tool to develop high-performance catalysts under practical
conditions. In our work, we have demonstrated a new Sr-mediated reconstruction method to realize
the finely design of metal-ion vacancy in dynamically reconstructed electrocatalysts under OER
conditions. Our work proved that the Sr-ion substitution in cobalt selenide pre-catalysts could
supply electrons more efficiently than Co atoms to bond Se sites to weaken Co-Se bond strength,
resulting in the much-lowered Co-Se bond dissociation energy to accelerate leaching of lattice Se
during OER reconstruction. Such the accelerated Se leaching could induce the much-lowered
coordination of adjacent Co sites and thus accelerate the leaching of lattice Co to form abundant
Co-ion vacancy in reconstructed CoOOH catalysts. As such, we have presented a new Sr-ion-
mediated reconstruction method to realize the finely design of metal-ion vacancy in dynamically
reconstructed electrocatalysts under OER conditions.
ii) We demonstrate the critical role of the well-defined Co-ion vacancy of dynamically
reconstructed CoOOH catalysts in altering the OER pathway for activity enhancement and refilling
lattice oxygen for stability strengthening. To overcome the theoretically limited OER overpotential
of 370 mV in traditional adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) for activity enhancement, it is
highly desired to trigger lattice-oxygen oxidation mechanism (LOM) by activating lattice oxygen.
However, the generated oxygen deficiencies due to the participation of lattice oxygen during LOM
route always render the dissolution of adjacent lattice metal with structure collapse, leading to the
degraded performance of catalysts under LOM route for long-term utilization. Accordingly, it is
challenging and fundamentally important to develop well-reconstructed Co-based catalysts under
OER conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen for active and stable OER.
Our work proved that the well-defined Co-ion vacancy in dynamically reconstructed CoOOH
catalysts can not only strengthen valence-electron sharing between Co and O sites with enhanced
Co-O covalency for lattice oxygen activation with triggered LOM route, but also promoted
valence-electron interaction between Co sites and OH adsorbates with enhanced hydroxyl affinity

E
The reaction order suggests how the OER kinetics depends on the proton activity. A zeroth-order
reaction implies no dependence, while a first-order reaction implies a linear dependence. The
reaction order would be zero if the reaction follows the concerted path, where the proton transfer
is not decoupled from the electron transfer. In contrast, the reaction order would be non-vanishing
if the transfer processes are decoupled. For the LOM and AEM routes of alkaline OER, it has been
well demonstrated the concerted proton-electron-transfer process of AEM route and the decoupled
proton-electron-transfer process of LOM route. As such, the reaction order, as obtained by
measuring the OER currents with different pH electrolyte, could be used to identify whether the
lattice oxygen participates in the OER process. The highly pH-dependent activities indicate the
non-zero reaction order, in accordance with the decoupled proton-electron-transfer process of
LOM route.

## Paper

## Abstract

Precisely engineering metal-ion vacancy in dynamically reconstructed electrocatalysts provides an attractive symmetry-breaking tool to develop robust electrocatalysts under operation conditions. Herein, we demonstrate a convenient Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction strategy to fabricate Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH nanosheets under oxygen evolution reaction conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen for practical anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis. The Sr-ion substitution in pre-catalysts can weaken bond strength for facilitated Co-ion vacancies formation in reconstructed oxyhydroxides. These Co-ion vacancies not only strengthen Co-O covalency for lattice oxygen activation, but also improve hydroxyl affinity for lattice oxygen refilling. The corresponding water electrolyzer exhibits a cutting-edge current of 3.3 A cm-2 at 2.0 V with a lowered energy consumption of 43.5 kWh kg-1 H2, and negligible degradation of 0.10 mV h-1 for 1000 h. This work paves an enlightening guideline to finely engineer metal-ion vacancy in dynamically reconstructed electrocatalysts, demonstrating the feasibility to develop targeted catalysts under practical conditions.

---

## Introduction

The anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) is becoming highly attractive for industrial hydrogen production due to its facility of combining advantages of alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) and proton-exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), such as employing earth-abundant catalysts and affording high operating currents1–3. Nevertheless, the industry-scale application of AEMWE is largely limited by the lack of non-noble metal-based catalysts with both high activity and stability for sluggish oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at anode4,5. Although several non-noble 3d metal-based materials have been reported to be active relative to commercial Ir- and Ru-based oxides, most of them still suffer from dynamic reconstruction with severe degradation under long-term OER conditions6–8. Specially, cobalt oxyhydroxide (CoOOH), known as the real catalytic phase reconstructed from pristine Co-based materials under OER conditions9–11, has been recently identified as one of the most promising OER catalysts for practical utilization with a relatively slow degradation rate and adjustable activity12,13. To overcome the theoretically limited OER overpotential of 370 mV in traditional adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM)14–16, activation of lattice oxygen by improving metal-oxygen covalency has been revealed to trigger lattice-oxygen oxidation mechanism (LOM) for activity enhancement17–19. However, the generated oxygen deficiencies due to the participation of lattice oxygen always render the dissolution of adjacent lattice metal with structure collapse, leading to the degraded performance of catalysts under LOM route for long-term utilization20–22. Accordingly, it is challenging and fundamentally important to develop well-reconstructed Co-based catalysts under OER conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen for practical AEMWE.

As a typical symmetry-breaking structure, the construction of metal-ion vacancies has been recently recognized to make an adjustment in the local atomic configuration of metal-based catalysts with altered charge density gradient, thus resulting in distinct catalytic behaviors23–25. For instance, Wang and co-workers demonstrated that the La-ion vacancy in LaFeO3 can greatly enhance the mobility of lattice oxygen due to the decreased electron density, subsequently reducing the barrier for C-H cleavage and oxidation of methane to generate syngas26. Of note, almost all the current efforts have been made to develop strategies to fabricate metal-ion vacancies in as-synthesized nanomaterials, while the inevitably dynamic reconstruction of metal-based catalysts under operation conditions could rebuild the local atomic structures with vanished vacancy sites27–29. For example, Magnussen et al. observed the dynamic reconstruction of Cu catalysts from low-coordinated Cu nanoclusters into isolated Cu atoms with increased potentials during electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR)30. Yang et al. proved the electrochemical reconstruction of Cu single atoms in C3N4 to Cu nanoparticles as the active phase for C2+ products during CO2RR31. As such, the precise design of metal-ion vacancies in dynamically reconstructed metal-based catalysts deserves to be investigated, which could serve as a versatile tool to develop high-performance catalysts under practical conditions.

Here, we demonstrate a facile Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction strategy to synthesize Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH nanosheets under OER conditions with balanced activation and refilling of lattice oxygen as efficient and stable anodic catalysts for practical AEMWE. Mechanistic investigations unveiled that Sr-ion substitution in selenide pre-catalysts could largely weaken the bond strength for accelerated reconstruction under OER conditions, contributing to the generation of abundant Co-ion vacancy in reconstructed oxyhydroxides. These Co-ion vacancies not only strengthened valence-electron sharing between Co and O sites with enhanced covalency for lattice oxygen activation with triggered LOM route, but also promoted valence-electron interaction between Co sites and OH adsorbates with enhanced hydroxyl affinity for lattice oxygen refilling during LOM route. Accordingly, these catalysts served as promising anodic OER catalysts for AEMWE. Relative to CoOOH and commercial RuO2, the Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH nanosheets showed an 18.6-fold and 25.0-fold increase in OER currents, respectively, as well as a significantly promoted OER stability with only 2% degradation in overpotentials after 10000 accelerated potential cycles. Practical testing in AEMWE presented a cutting-edge cell voltage of 2.0 V to achieve 3.3 A cm−2 with a lowered energy consumption of 43.5 kWh kg−1 H2, and a good operation stability with a negligible degradation rate of 0.10 mV h−1 for 1000 h, outperforming commercial RuO2. The competitive AEMWE performance further identified the compatibility of Co-vacancy-enriched Sr-CoOOH for practical utilization.

---

## Results

To begin with, Sr-ion-substituted CoSe2 nanobelts with weakened bond strength (denoted as Sr-CoSe2-w) were synthesized and serve as the pre-catalysts before electrochemical reconstruction (Fig. 1a). As theoretically calculated in the well-established Sr-ion-substituted CoSe2 and pure CoSe2 models (Supplementary Fig. 1), the Co-Se bond length around Sr sites exhibited an obvious increase (Supplementary Fig. 2a), together with the decreased Se vacancy formation energy with Sr substitution (Supplementary Fig. 2b), suggesting the weakened Co-Se bonding by Sr substitution. These selenides possessed smooth and belt-like morphology with uniform distribution of Co, Se, and Sr, as identified by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Fig. 1b), and high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) with elemental mapping (Fig. 1c). The Sr/Co molar ratio was determined as 1.0% by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). The aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM image clearly suggested the well-maintained cubic CoSe2 structure of 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w32, where the Sr-ion substitution can be confirmed by the intensity profiles of selected region (Fig. 1d). Similarly, by varying added amounts of precursors, 0.6%Sr-CoSe2-w, 0.2%Sr-CoSe2-w and pure CoSe2 pre-catalysts with uniform morphology and cubic phase were obtained (Supplementary Fig. 3). The Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra and fitting results demonstrated the largely reduced Co-Se coordination from 3.9 for pure CoSe2 to 2.3 for 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w, as well as the obviously increased Co-Se bond length after Sr substitution (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 1). These results clearly suggested the largely weakened bond strength in these selenides through Sr-ion substitution. To deeply understand the weakened Co-Se bond caused by Sr-ion substitution, the valence-electron states were analyzed. The Co 2p X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum for 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w exhibited two typical peaks at 778.5 eV and 793.4 eV that assigned to Co-Se bond in cubic CoSe233. Obviously, a negative shift of Co 2p peaks to low energy was observed on going from pure CoSe2 to 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w (Fig. 1f), indicating the enriched valence-electron density of Co sites with Sr-ion substitution. Meanwhile, a positive shift of Sr 3d XPS peaks of Sr-Se bond was also found with increased Sr/Co ratio from 0.2% to 1.0% (Supplementary Fig. 4)34. These results suggested the substituted Sr atoms in selenide pre-catalysts could supply electrons more efficiently than Co atoms to bond Se sites, in accordance with the difference of work functions, thus accounting for the weakened Co-Se bond strength.

The weakened bond strength in Sr-CoSe2-w pre-catalysts endowed a lowered dissociation energy of Co-Se bond relative to that in pure CoSe235,36, which could accelerate the bond dissociation under the attack of OH- ions from alkaline electrolyte with forming low-coordinated Co sites during reconstruction, reasonably facilitating the formation of abundant Co-ion vacancies in the reconstructed oxyhydroxide catalysts (Fig. 2a). To clarify the reconstruction process, in situ Raman analysis was conducted under a series of potential cycles (Supplementary Fig. 5). As shown in Fig. 2b, the Raman spectra of pristine 1.0%Sr-CoSe2-w pre-catalysts showcased three typical peaks at 476, 517 and 683 cm−1 assigned to cubic CoSe2 phase37. As the potential cycles proceeded, these peaks tended to vanish, together with the formation of another two peaks at 498 and 594 cm−1 assigned to Eg and A1g vibrational modes of Co-O in CoOOH (Supplementary Fig. 6)38, as well as the gradually elevated Co oxidation state to ~3 (Fig. 2c), manifesting the complete reconstruction from selenide to oxyhydroxide phase. Relative to the pre-catalysts without Sr-ion substitution, the Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction can be notably accelerated, as proved by the obviously reduced potential cycles for reconstruction. The morphology of reconstructed oxyhydroxides was characterized by TEM (Fig. 2d), where interconnected nanosheets with massive boundaries were observed. Such boundaries could facilitate the generation of low-coordination vacancies in these Sr-ion-substituted oxyhydroxide nanosheets39. For simplicity, we designated them as Sr-CoOOH nanosheets. The STEM image and element mapping exhibited homogeneous distribution of Co and Sr in these nanosheets (Fig. 2e), where the Sr/Co ratio was maintained as 1.0% by ICP-OES. The atomic structure was further visualized by an aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM image (Fig. 2f). The bright spots marked by yellow circles clearly suggested the substituted Sr atoms, while the diffraction rings in the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern suggested the amorphous structure. The atomic dispersion of these Sr atoms could also be verified by the absence of Sr-Sr coordination in Sr K-edge EXAFS spectra (Fig. 2g). Similar morphology and amorphous structures were also observed in other reconstructed Sr-CoOOH nanosheets with maintained Sr/Co ratios of 0.2% and 0.6%, as evidenced by the TEM images, HRTEM images, XRD patterns and ICP-OES analysis (Supplementary Figs. 7, 8).

To verify the local coordination environment in these Sr-CoOOH nanosheets, Co K-edge EXAFS measurements were conducted (Fig. 2h). All the Sr-CoOOH nanosheets exhibited two main peaks at around 1.5 Å and 2.5 Å, attributing to Co-O and Co-Co bonds for CoOOH, respectively40. Notably, with increased Sr contents, a shrinkage of Co-O bond length was observed, suggesting the enhanced Co-O covalency. The strengthened Co-O covalency could efficiently activate lattice oxygen to trigger the LOM pathway for bypassing the theoretically limited OER overpotential41. Meanwhile, least-squares fittings were performed to quantitatively understand the coordination structure (Supplementary Table 2). As collected in Fig. 2i, the Co-Co coordination numbers decreased from 3.0 for CoOOH to 2.7 for 0.2%Sr-CoOOH, 2.6 for 0.6%Sr-CoOOH, and 2.4 for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, together with the well-maintained Co-O coordination numbers, clearly demonstrating the formation of abundant Co vacancies by Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction. In addition, such the construction of metal-ion vacancies by Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction could also be extended to other reconstructed metal-based materials (Supplementary Figs. 9, 10 and Table 3), suggesting the Sr-ion-mediated reconstruction method as a useful tool to realize metal-ion vacancies in dynamically reconstructed catalysts.

The valence electron properties of the Sr-CoOOH nanosheets were characterized by XPS analysis. As shown in Fig. 2j, the Co 2p3/2 XPS peaks at 779.9 eV and 781.1 eV corresponded to the Co3+ cations in CoOOH42, while a positive shift of Co 2p peaks to high energy was observed from pure CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH. Meanwhile, the Sr 3d XPS spectra, which were divided into two peaks at 133.4 and 135.1 eV for Sr cations43 and in accordance with the cationic nature from Sr K-edge XANES spectra (Supplementary Fig. 11a), showed a negative shift to low energy from 0.2%Sr-CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH (Supplementary Fig. 11b). The decreased valence-electron density of Co sites and increased valence-electron density of Sr sites implied enhanced valence-electron interaction of Co-O bonds in Sr-CoOOH (Supplementary Table 4), in accordance with the elevated Co-O covalency. The electron state of O sites was studied by O 1s XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 12), which could be fitted into four contributions from O-Co bonds (529.7 eV), OH-Co bonds (530.8 eV), low-coordination O (OL, 531.5 eV) and adsorbed water (H2Oad, 532.1 eV)44. The corresponding contents were collected in Fig. 2k. Of note, an obvious increase of O-Co bonds can be observed from pure CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, which could be attributed to the enhanced Co-O covalency and elevated structure stabilization due to the higher bond dissociation energy of Sr-O bond (454 kJ mol−1) than Co-O bond (368 kJ mol−1)45. The decreased OH-Co bonds and retained low-coordination O consisted with the increased Co vacancies and retained Co-O coordination from CoOOH to 1.0%Sr-CoOOH. Moreover, the increased O contents for water adsorption indicated the elevated affinity of oxygenous species of Sr-CoOOH, which could accelerate the refilling process of lattice oxygen during OER.

The electrocatalytic OER performance of all the Sr-CoOOH catalysts were investigated in O2-saturated 1 M KOH electrolyte. As illustrated by the polarization curves in Fig. 3a, which were all corrected for the ohmic loss (Supplementary Fig. 13), 1.0%Sr-CoOOH exhibited the earliest onset potential and an overpotential as low as 255 mV at 10 mA cm−2, significantly outperforming that of 312 mV for pure CoOOH and 327 mV for commercial RuO2. Notably, 1.0%Sr-CoOOH can achieve the current density of 100 mA cm−2 with a low overpotential of 293 mV (Fig. 3b), which was 5.0, 8.8, 18.6, and 25.0 times higher than that for 0.6%Sr-CoOOH, 0.2%Sr-CoOOH, pure CoOOH, and commercial RuO2, respectively. Meanwhile, the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, achieved by the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) measurements (Supplementary Figs. 14, 15), showed only the 1.1, 1.8, and 2.7-fold increase relative to that for 0.6%Sr-CoOOH, 0.2%Sr-CoOOH, and pure CoOOH, respectively. Obviously, the current increase for these samples was much larger than the variation of ECSA, suggesting the remarkably enhanced intrinsic activity. The activity elevation was further verified by the Tafel plot and turnover frequency (TOF) analysis. Figure 3c displays a much lowered Tafel slope of 38 mV dec−1 for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH relative to 0.6%Sr-CoOOH (46 mV dec−1), 0.2%Sr-CoOOH (65 mV dec−1), CoOOH (70 mV dec−1) and commercial RuO2 (117 mV dec−1), indicating the accelerated reaction kinetics. The TOF values for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH also remained higher than those for all the tested samples throughout applied potentials, further implying the intrinsically boosted OER activity (Fig. 3d). Of note, the OER activity of 1.0%Sr-CoOOH was competitive (Supplementary Table 5), and could further afford a more competitive target on the gas diffusion electrode with a significantly lowered overpotential of 198 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and a Tafel slope of 32 mV dec−1 as the efficient Co-based OER catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 16).

The stability of these Sr-CoOOH catalysts under OER conditions were systematically elucidated. To understand the operating stability, we conducted galvanostatic start-stop measurements at 10 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3e). For 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, the voltages at 10 mA cm−2 showed neglectable variation during repeated start-stop tests, implying the attractive stability for practical operation46. The long-term stability was assessed by means of accelerated voltammetry cycling tests (Fig. 3f). In comparison with the significantly degraded activities of pure CoOOH under long-term cycling, the activity of 1.0%Sr-CoOOH showed negligible variation after 10000 potential cycles. As quantitatively summarized in Fig. 3g, the overpotentials for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH to achieve 10 mA cm−2 only exhibited a 2% increase after 10000 scan cycles, much lower than the 35% increase in overpotentials for pure CoOOH and thus indicating the high stability of Sr-CoOOH for long-term utilization. The dissolution of metal ions under different scan cycles was also measured by ICP-OES to further evaluate the stability (Fig. 3h). For pure CoOOH, Co components dissolved obviously after 2000 cycles and showed a 49% decrease in content after 10000 cycles. For 1.0%Sr-CoOOH, these Co components were basically retained during the long-term cycling with only 4% decrease in content after 10000 cycles, clearly suggesting the improved stability of Sr-CoOOH. The structural stability was further demonstrated by the well-maintained Sr/Co molar ratios in 1.0%Sr-CoOOH during long-term cycling, as well as the well-maintained morphology from TEM image (Supplementary Fig. 17a), amorphous phase from HRTEM image (Supplementary Fig. 17b) and XRD patterns (Supplementary Fig. 17c), and stable valence states of Co, Sr, O sites from XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 17d–f). The high stability of 1.0%Sr-CoOOH also ensured sufficient exposure of active sites for long-term OER catalysis, as verified by the well-maintained ECSAs during long-term cycling (Supplementary Figs. 18, 19 and Fig. 3i).

Considering the enhanced Co-O covalency can trigger the switch of OER route from AEM to LOM for activity improvement, the reaction mechanism for these Sr-CoOOH catalysts were experimentally evaluated. Figure 4a shows the in situ Raman spectra for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH during the real-time OER process with applied potentials. At the open-circuit potential (OCP), two typical peaks at 498 and 594 cm−1 were visible, in accordance with Co-O stretching of amorphous CoOOH. When the applied potential increased, these two peaks shifted to 477 and 574 cm−1 as the Co-O stretching of CoO247, together with the generation of a new peak at 1064 cm−1 for superoxide O-O bands with the participation of lattice oxygen48, suggesting the occurrence of the LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH containing the deprotonation and immediate coupling with lattice oxygen. For comparison, potential-dependent Raman spectra for pure CoOOH were also detected (Fig. 4b). The absence of peaks at around 1064 cm−1 indicated the different OER pathway for pure CoOOH from the LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH. Besides, the variation of Co sites could also be verified by XANES spectra (Supplementary Fig. 20), where the increased oxidation states of Co with applied potentials were clearly observed. Of note, with applied potential back to OCP, both of these samples exhibited a reversed Co oxidation state to ~3, together with the well-maintained coordination structure around Co sites (Supplementary Fig. 21 and Table 6, 7), suggesting the stable Co active sites in these oxyhydroxide catalysts for the OER process. To further identify the OER route, the pH-dependent activities were tested. With pH values decreased from 14.0 to 12.5, the OER activities for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH exhibited a significant decrease (Fig. 4c), while pure CoOOH only showed a tiny variation (Fig. 4d). To precisely clarify the correlation between pH and activity, the proton reaction order on RHE scale (ρRHE) was calculated (Fig. 4e), where the concerted proton-electron-transfer process tends to be zeroth-order49. Notably, the ρRHE value of 0.84 for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH was much larger than that of 0.04 for pure CoOOH, suggesting the triggered LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH from the AEM route for CoOOH50–52. Furthermore, to track the O-O coupling species generated with a negative charge in a non-concerted proton-electron-transfer LOM route, tetramethylammonium cation (TMA+) was introduced into the electrolyte as a probe due to its specific interaction with negative oxygenated species for hindered OER kinetics53. As shown in Fig. 4f, the 1.0%Sr-CoOOH showed obviously reduced OER activity in 1 M TMAOH relative to 1 M KOH, together with the increased Tafel slope from 38 to 65 mV dec−1, confirming the LOM route occurred with strong binding of TMA+ on O2- species. For pure CoOOH, only a slight change in activities was observed (Fig. 4g), indicating the AEM route. The binding behaviors of TMA+ were also detected by Raman spectra (Fig. 4h). Besides the two peaks at 498 and 594 cm–1 referring to CoOOH phase for both samples, two new peaks at 752 and 954 cm−1 corresponding to TMA+ were only observed on 1.0%Sr-CoOOH under 1.50 V in TMAOH54, further indicating the switched LOM route for 1.0%Sr-CoOOH from AEM route for pure CoOOH (Fig. 4i).

To gain an in-depth understanding on the intrinsic reason for switching pathway with activity enhancement as well as the improvement of stability, we conducted first-principles calculations using DFT. The models of Sr-CoOOH and pure CoOOH were well-established in Supplementary Data 1, Figs. 22, 23, and Table 8, where another Sr-CoOOH flat surface without Co vacancy was also constructed for comparison, and denoted as Sr-CoOOHf. Figure 5a shows the change of valence-electron density of Co sites in these structures. The inhomogeneity of electron loss at each Co sites in pure CoOOH could be attributed to the Jahn-Teller distortion. Relative to pure CoOOH, the Sr substitution in Sr-CoOOHf induced increased electron loss from adjacent Co sites, which could be attributed to the limited valence-electron providing ability of Sr to bond O and thus the increased valence-electron supply from adjacent Co sites. As such, further introduction of Co vacancy would induce extra valence-electron supply from adjacent Co sites to bond O, which was also suggested by the extra electron loss of Co sites in Sr-CoOOHv. The increased valence-electron sharing between Co and O could reasonably shorten the adjacent Co-O bonds (Supplementary Fig. 24) with enhanced covalency, in accordance with the XPS and EXAFS results. The enhanced Co-O covalency was further verified by the projected density of states (pDOS) with averaging the potential Co and O sites (Supplementary Fig. 25). As presented in Fig. 5b, relative to pure CoOOH, the Sr substitution in Sr-CoOOHf could diminish the difference between Co 3d band center (εd) and O 2p band center (εp) from 0.335 eV to 0.167 eV, indicating the partially promoted covalency. Meanwhile, with further introduction of Co vacancy in Sr-CoOOHv, the d band of Co and p band of O exhibited a further shortened band-center difference of 0.127 eV, indicating that the Co vacancy could enhance the Co-O covalency and thus lead to the efficient lattice oxygen activation for triggering the LOM pathway. The reaction sites for LOM could be further verified by calculating the energy difference of the potential-determining step (PDS, Supplementary Fig. 26). In view of the obvious difference of step I between AEM and LOM pathways (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 27), the activation barriers from the AEM intermediate of adsorbed O after step I to the LOM intermediate after step I for O-O coupling were then assessed to clarify the switch difficulty of OER pathways. As shown in Fig. 5d, the energy barrier from AEM intermediate to the isomeric LOM intermediate after step I was 0.51 eV for Sr-CoOOHv, obviously lower than that of 1.52 eV for Sr-CoOOHf and 1.68 eV for pure CoOOH (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 28), and thus indicating the facilitated switch of OER route from AEM to LOM for Sr-CoOOHv with rich Co vacancies. The switched route from AEM to LOM because of the lattice oxygen activation could boost the theoretically plagued OER kinetics by overcoming the linear relation of OH* and OOH* with direct O-O coupling55. To clarify the role of the altered OER pathway in activity, the relevant Gibbs free energies for reaction steps on Sr-CoOOHv and CoOOH were further depicted. For both structures in Fig. 5f, g, the deprotonation of OH* (step I) in the AEM route or the deprotonation of OH* with immediate O-O coupling (step I) in the LOM route could serve as the potential-determining step. For CoOOH, the energy barrier of 2.01 eV of PDS in the AEM route was lower than that of 2.63 eV in the LOM route, suggesting the OER process follows the AEM route. A similar AEM route could also be observed for Sr-CoOOHf (Supplementary Fig. 29), identifying the deficient activation of lattice oxygen only by Sr substitution. In contrast, for Sr-CoOOHv, the PDS energy in the AEM route was higher than that in the LOM pathway, even under varied U values (Supplementary Fig. 30), reflecting the switched LOM route for Sr-CoOOHv. Moreover, the well-established Sr-CoOOHv exhibited an obviously lowered PDS energy barrier of 1.58 eV than that of 2.01 eV for pure CoOOH, as well as those for the other configurations with varied position of Co vacancy sites (Supplementary Figs. 31, 32), indicating the intrinsically accelerated OER process for Sr-CoOOHv with switched LOM route.

Considering the release of lattice oxygen involving in the LOM route would dynamically generate oxygen deficiencies in catalysts and result in structural collapse, it is of significant importance to efficiently refill these lattice oxygen deficiencies during the LOM route for long-term stability56. Accordingly, the behaviors for lattice oxygen refilling in the LOM route on Sr-CoOOHv and CoOOH were analyzed. Relative to pure CoOOH, the Co-Co coordination missing in Sr-CoOOHv with abundant Co vacancies and Sr substitution with limited valence-electron providing ability could narrow the d band of adjacent Co sites due to the reduced Co d-band overlap, as verified by the upshifted d-band center (Fig. 5b) and the calculated d-band width57, and thus leading to the strengthened OH adsorption affinity for Sr-CoOOHv. To clearly understand the behaviors for lattice oxygen refilling in the LOM route, the electron density differences of intermediate structures of Sr-CoOOHv and CoOOH for lattice oxygen refilling with OH adsorbates were analyzed. As illustrated in Fig. 5h, relative to pure CoOOH, the Co vacancy in Sr-CoOOHv could trigger an enhanced valence-electron interaction between adjacent Co sites and OH adsorbates to refill the lattice oxygen deficiency generated during the LOM route, indicating the promoted lattice oxygen refilling ability of Sr-CoOOHv with Co vacancies. The efficient lattice oxygen refilling was further verified by the energy barrier calculation (Fig. 5i). Notably, the Sr-CoOOHv still exhibited a lower energy barrier of 0.79 eV for incorporating O into the lattice than that of 1.20 eV for pure CoOOH, suggesting the efficient refilling ability of lattice oxygen of Sr-CoOOHv and thus the strengthened OER stability. The structure stability under OER conditions could be further proved by the electrochemical phase diagram58–60, where Sr-CoOOHv could exhibit obviously enhanced stability with much-lowered formation free energy with respect to pure CoOOH (Supplementary Fig. 33).

The boosted activity with efficient lattice oxygen activation and strengthened stability with efficient lattice oxygen refilling of Sr-CoOOHv suggest its attractive potential for realistic utilization as anodic OER catalysts. To this end, we conducted the tests in an anion-exchange membrane electrolyzer at 80 °C with 1 M KOH as feed and commercial Pt/C as cathodic catalysts (Supplementary Figs. 34, 35). Polarization curves were collected in Fig. 6a. Notably, the AEMWE with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode achieved a remarkably high current density of 3.3 A cm−2 with a much-lowered voltage of 2.0 V, clearly outperforming the pure CoOOH anode with a current density of 1.9 A cm−2 at 2.0 V, as well as the commercial RuO2 anode with a current density of 0.63 A cm−2 at 2.0 V. Moreover, at 1.0 A cm−2, the AEMWE with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode produced 1.78 L of H2 at the running electrolyzer for 1 h. The energy consumption of the AEMWE device was deduced to be 43.5 kWh kg−1 H2 (Fig. 6b), obviously lower than that of CoOOH and the goal of 47.9 kWh kg−1 H2 from the Office of Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy (EERE) in the US Department of Energy (DOE). The Faradaic efficiency of O2 product in the AEMWE device with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode was quantified as a near unity value of 99.3% (Fig. 6c), suggesting the entire consumption of charge without parasitic reactions. To further confirm the applicability of the electrolyzer assembled with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv, the operating stability measurements were performed in AEMWE at a constant industrial-level current density of 500 mA cm−2 under 80 °C. As shown in Fig. 6d, the AEMWE with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode presented a well-maintained performance during 1000 h electrolysis with a negligible degradation rate of 0.10 mV h−1, significantly lower than that of 1.33 mV h−1 during 95 h electrolysis on a commercial RuO2 anode and implying the improved stability. The overall performance of the AEMWE device with 1.0%Sr-CoOOHv anode, including current density at 2.0 V, operating time and degradation rate, were competitive with using a commercial anion-exchange membrane and a commercial Pt/C cathode (Supplementary Table 9).
